name: Design a Data Warehouse
intent: Answer analytical questions over ten billion rows in seconds by storing data by column, skipping what a query does not need, and spreading the work over many machines.
codeTitle: a column store with date partitions and zone maps
finalIntro: One dashboard query over the last week of sales, and then the same dashboard again.
prompt: Design the analytical database for an online retailer. The production database holds about 10 billion order-line rows from three years, growing by 9 million a day, with 20 or more columns each. Analysts and dashboards ask questions such as revenue by country by day, top products in a category, and customer retention by month. Hundreds of queries can be running at once, and the data should be no more than about 15 minutes old.
functional: Run SQL aggregations, joins and group-bys over the whole history
Load changes continuously from production databases and event streams
Model the data as facts and dimensions that analysts can join
Serve scheduled dashboards and ad-hoc exploration at the same time
Keep history, accept late data and corrections, and reload a day when it was wrong
nonFunctional: A typical dashboard query over billions of rows returns in a few seconds, and a heavy one within minutes
Data in the warehouse is at most about 15 minutes behind production
Cost follows the bytes a query reads, so it must be predictable and controllable
Hundreds of concurrent queries, where one huge query cannot starve the dashboards
Storage grows to petabytes and is durable, and compute can be resized without moving data
A query sees a consistent snapshot even while a load is running

firstAttempt.text: Point the dashboards at a read replica of the production database. The orders table has B-tree indexes on a few columns, and queries join it to the product and customer tables. The analysts write SQL against the same schema the application uses.
limits: A row store keeps all 20 columns of a row together, so summing one column still reads every byte of the table, about 2 TB
An index helps with finding a few rows, but a report that touches millions of rows does better with a sequential scan, and the index does not make that scan any smaller
One machine reads, decompresses and aggregates the data, so a big query takes minutes and cannot be sped up by adding more machines
A long report and the load of replicated changes compete on the same replica, and one analyst's query can slow every dashboard
The application schema is normalised for writes, so each question needs many joins over big tables

steps.title: Store each column on its own, and compress it
steps.problem: Analytical queries read a few columns of billions of rows. A row store keeps all the columns of a row together on disk, so adding up one column still reads every byte of every row, and its tuple-at-a-time execution is slow too.
steps.fix: Store each column in its own file, in blocks of tens of thousands of values, so a query opens only the columns it names. A file holds values of one type, which compress very well. Dictionary encoding replaces repeated strings such as a country with small integers, run-length encoding stores a sorted column as (value, count) pairs, delta encoding stores timestamps and ids as small differences, and a general compressor such as LZ4 or Zstandard goes on top. The engine processes a block of values at a time (vectorised execution, using SIMD instructions) and can often work on encoded data directly, such as counting a run without expanding it.
steps.tradeoff: Summing one column of 10 billion rows now reads a few gigabytes instead of 2 TB, and the same data takes a quarter of the space or less. Putting a whole row back together (select *) needs a read from every column file, and changing one row means rewriting a block, so this layout is for large, append-heavy reads and not for transactions.

steps.title: Partition by date, sort, and skip with zone maps
steps.problem: Even if it reads only one column, a query about the last week should not have to touch three years of data.
steps.fix: Cut the table into partitions by date, one per day, and sort the rows inside each partition by a sort key such as the country and then the customer. Every file records a zone map: the minimum and maximum of each column for each block. The planner reads these small summaries from a catalog first and skips every partition or block whose range cannot match the filter, so a 7-day filter reads 7 of 1,095 partitions. Sorting makes the ranges tight, so filters on the sort key skip blocks too, and it creates long runs that run-length encoding turns into a few bytes. Files are kept large, from 128 MB up to 1 GB.
steps.tradeoff: A query on a recent week reads under 1% of the data, and its cost falls by the same factor. Only filters on the partition and sort columns benefit: for an unsorted column every block's min and max span the whole range, so nothing is skipped. Too many tiny partitions make the metadata and file opens the bottleneck, and a table can be sorted only one way.

steps.title: Run on many workers in parallel, and shuffle for joins
steps.problem: A single machine reads a few GB per second at best. A query that must read hundreds of gigabytes, decompress them and aggregate them takes minutes, however well the data is laid out.
steps.fix: A coordinator parses and plans the SQL and splits it into fragments, which run on many worker nodes at once (massively parallel processing), each on its own subset of the files. A group-by runs in two phases: each worker first sums its own rows into partial results, then the partials are shuffled over the network by a hash of the group key, so one worker owns each group and merges the pieces. A join of two big tables shuffles both of them by the join key. A join with a small dimension table is cheaper, because the small table is broadcast to every worker, and tables distributed on the same key can be joined with no shuffle at all.
steps.tradeoff: Scan time falls almost in proportion to the number of workers, since 16 nodes reading 1 GB/s each read 16 GB/s. The shuffle is the new cost: it uses the network, a hot key can overload one worker while the others wait, and the slowest worker decides when the query ends. The coordination also costs a fixed fraction of a second, which dominates small queries.

steps.title: Separate storage from compute, and cache
steps.problem: If the data lives on the workers' own disks, more storage means more nodes, an idle cluster still costs money, resizing means moving data, and a dead node has to be rebuilt before the data is safe again.
steps.fix: Keep the files in an object store, which is cheap, durable, replicated across zones and practically unlimited. Workers become stateless: they can be started, resized or stopped at any moment, and several clusters can read the same tables. Each worker caches the blocks it read recently on a local NVMe SSD, so hot data comes at several GB/s instead of the few hundred MB/s of a request to the object store. A transactional catalog records which files make up each version of a table, so a reader sees one consistent snapshot while a loader adds files.
steps.tradeoff: Storage and compute scale and are paid for separately, a cluster can shrink to zero, and losing a node loses only a cache. The first read of cold data is slower, each request to the object store has a latency of tens of milliseconds, so files must be large and read in parallel, and the shuffle still goes over the network.

steps.title: Load in micro-batches, transform in the warehouse, model as a star
steps.problem: Data arrives all day from the production database and from event streams. Inserting row by row into a column store creates millions of tiny files, and the raw application tables need many joins for every question.
steps.fix: Capture changes from the production database and events from a stream, and let a loader buffer them and write one columnar file per micro-batch, every minute or so, added to the table by a single atomic commit. A compaction job merges small files later. Raw data lands first and is transformed inside the warehouse with SQL (ELT) instead of in a separate cluster (ETL). The result is a star schema: a large fact table with one row per order line, holding keys and numeric measures, surrounded by small dimension tables for product, customer, store and date, which hold the descriptions. Slowly changing dimensions keep history by adding a new row with validity dates.
steps.tradeoff: Data is minutes old, the warehouse's own parallelism does the transformation, and a question needs a join or two on narrow numeric columns. Smaller batches give fresher data but more small files, late data and corrections need an upsert or a reload of a partition, and the model has to be designed with the questions in mind.

steps.title: Pre-aggregate common questions, and isolate the workloads
steps.problem: Hundreds of dashboards ask the same few questions every minute, and recomputing each of them from billions of rows is wasteful. One analyst's huge query can also slow every dashboard.
steps.fix: A materialised view stores the result of a common aggregation, such as revenue by country by day, which is a few hundred thousand rows, and is refreshed incrementally as new files arrive. The planner rewrites a matching query to read the view. Workloads are separated: dashboards, ad-hoc analysis, loading and data science each get their own cluster, or a queue with a share of the slots and a concurrency limit, and every query has a timeout and a cap on the bytes it may scan. A result cache returns the stored answer to an identical query while the data has not changed.
steps.tradeoff: Dashboards answer in milliseconds and a heavy query can no longer starve them. Views cost storage and refresh compute, only help with questions that were expected, and can lag behind the base table. Isolation can leave one cluster idle while another is saturated, which autoscaling and per-query limits only soften.

failures.scenario: A worker dies in the middle of a query
failures.impact: Its share of the work is lost, and a query that has been running for minutes would have to start again.
failures.answer: The coordinator notices through missed heartbeats and re-runs the failed fragments on other workers. Any worker can read any file from the object store, so nothing needs to be recovered, and only the cache on the dead node is cold. Long queries save their intermediate results so that a retry does not repeat everything.

failures.scenario: One key has far more rows than the others in a join
failures.impact: A null customer id or one huge customer holds 30% of the rows, so one worker gets 30% of the work while 15 others finish early and wait for it.
failures.answer: Statistics show the skew. The planner then broadcasts the smaller side, filters nulls before the join, handles the hot key separately, or salts it so that it spreads over several workers. Aggregating before the join, so that fewer rows are shuffled, helps too.

failures.scenario: Someone runs select * on the fact table with no filter
failures.impact: It reads about 2 TB, costs around $10, takes minutes and slows the queries that share the cluster.
failures.answer: The tool shows an estimate of the bytes before the query runs. Large tables can require a partition filter, each queue has a byte cap and a timeout, and ad-hoc queries run on their own cluster, so the damage stays in that queue. A cost alert tells the owner when a workload goes over its budget.

failures.scenario: A load fails halfway, or runs twice
failures.impact: Queries could see half a day of data, or the same orders twice, and every total would be wrong.
failures.answer: A load adds its files in one atomic commit to the catalog, so readers see all of a batch or none of it. Each batch has an id that the loader records, so a repeated batch is recognised and skipped. A day that turns out to be wrong is fixed by writing the corrected partition and replacing the old one in one commit.

alternatives.title: How the table is laid out

options.name: Row store (an ordinary database)
options.pro: Fast point lookups and updates of whole rows, and no extra system to run
options.con: Reads every column of every row it touches, so scans of billions of rows are slow and costly

options.name: Column store
options.pro: Reads only the needed columns, and compresses 3 to 10 times
options.con: Slow for single-row lookups and updates, and select * loses most of the benefit

options.name: Hybrid: rows for recent data, columns for history
options.pro: Handles fresh writes and big scans in one system
options.con: Two formats to maintain and a more complex engine

alternatives.pick: A column store for analytics, fed from the row-based production database.

alternatives.title: Where storage and compute live

options.name: Shared-nothing: data on the workers' disks
options.pro: Fast local reads, with no object store requests
options.con: Resizing moves data, storage and compute cannot scale independently, and the cluster costs money when idle

options.name: Object store plus stateless workers with a cache
options.pro: Independent scaling, clusters can stop, and several clusters share one copy
options.con: Cold reads are slower, and caching has to be good

options.name: Serverless: slots allocated per query
options.pro: Nothing to size, and you pay per query
options.con: Less control over performance, and a cost that follows the bytes scanned

alternatives.pick: Object store plus workers with SSD caches, with separate clusters per workload.

alternatives.title: How data is loaded

options.name: Nightly batch ETL
options.pro: Simple, with large efficient files and an easy reload
options.con: Data is up to a day old

options.name: Micro-batches every minute or so, ELT
options.pro: Data is minutes old and files are still reasonably large
options.con: Needs compaction, and exactly-once loading takes care

options.name: Stream into a real-time OLAP engine
options.con: A different system to run, with more limited joins and SQL

alternatives.pick: Micro-batches into the warehouse, and a real-time engine only for the few dashboards that need seconds.

alternatives.title: How the data is modelled

options.name: Star schema
options.pro: Few joins, small dimensions that can be broadcast, and easy for analysts to understand
options.con: Needs design and a transformation step, and changes in dimensions need handling

options.name: One wide denormalised table
options.pro: No joins, and columnar compression absorbs the repetition
options.con: A change to a dimension rewrites many rows, and the table is very wide

options.name: The normalised application schema
options.con: Many joins for each question, and the schema changes whenever the application does

alternatives.pick: A star schema, with a wide table built on top of it where one hot dashboard needs it.

roles.description: People and tools that send SQL.

roles.label: Query entry
roles.description: The coordinator that plans queries, and the queues that admit them.

roles.label: Loading pipeline
roles.description: The loader that turns changes into files in micro-batches.

roles.label: Workers
roles.description: The parallel nodes that scan, aggregate and join.

roles.label: Storage and metadata
roles.description: Column files, zone maps, caches and materialised views.
